Text | Like Jiang

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Using VR in architecture, landscape and urban design is nothing new. VR, especially online VR, makes it easy to share design intentions and results with clients, governments and the public in an intuitive, interactive way. Over the past ten or twenty years, however, these applications have dealt almost exclusively with the visual. They offer visualization only, or add illustrative sound that does not strictly match the virtual scene. Sound, including noise and the wider soundscape, is an important part of the urban environment and ought to be built into these VR applications, so that designs can be presented more effectively and the public can take part more fully.

To do this, auralization is an essential technology (for more on auralization, see A history of acoustics: auralization). Applications of auralization in planning, design and public participation, whether on its own or combined with visualization, are few compared with visualization alone, but there are some. They fall broadly into four categories: offline with non-real-time rendering, online with non-real-time rendering, offline with real-time rendering, and online with real-time rendering. Non-real-time auralization is fairly mature by now; one example is the auralization and visualization of railway noise by the team behind the EU DESTINATE project [1]. Real-time rendering, online or offline, is much rarer. High-quality real-time auralization is genuinely hard. Unlike light in visualization, sound in auralization travels far more slowly. In a complex space, the direct sound from multiple sources reaches the ear with delays, and the sound is reflected and attenuated many times between surfaces, so sound propagation is hard to simulate both accurately and quickly. And that is before you take into account the wave nature of sound, source directivity and binaural effects. Online real-time rendering is harder still. Yet without real-time auralization, there is no way to bring sound into interactive VR.

In fact, as early as 2016, I (then in Italy) and Fanyu Meng (then in Germany) attempted online real-time auralization combined with visualization. It was, of course, only a demonstration, a proof of concept. The project was a subproject of SONORUS – Urban Sound Planning, under the EU’s Marie Curie program (the results of SONORUS were compiled into a booklet [2]).

My reasons for wanting online real-time auralization plus visualization were very simple. First, the project required VR, so the rendering had to be real time. Second, I did not want to recruit people for lab experiments, because the Italian university I was at did not allow research funds to be spent on recruiting participants. My first study with lab experiments had been a nightmare: participants had to drive themselves to a lab out in the countryside and then, with temperatures above 30 °C, sit in a stuffy anechoic chamber with no air conditioning or fan, wearing a VR headset and listening to all kinds of traffic noise. (My thanks to my Italian colleagues at the time, who found most of the participants for me.) After that, I was determined never to run lab experiments again. Having been a teenager hooked on World of Warcraft, I thought: why not build something like an online game? Game engines such as Unity and Unreal Engine could already do simple online real-time sound rendering, but that did not count as auralization, because it did not involve synthesizing the sound sources. I didn’t have the skills to synthesize sources myself, and nor did anyone on our project team in Italy. But as luck would have it, I met Fanyu Meng at a conference in Portugal and lost no time in roping him in.

We used Piazza Vittoria in Naples as our case study site. Figures 1 and 2 compare the real scene with the scene in VR. Figure 3 shows the basic framework, workflow, software, hardware and materials. Here I will focus on how the sound material was generated, collected and rendered.

Figure 1. The real scene compared with the scene in VR (a)

Figure 2. The real scene compared with the scene in VR (b)

Figure 3. The basic framework, workflow, software, hardware and materials of the web-based VR of Naples

In our project, the sound material fell into four types, according to how it was obtained:

1. Synthesized signals. Each car is a moving point source, and the noise each one produces at the source position was synthesized (Fanyu Meng will cover source synthesis in a later article). With the right resources, you could also record car noise at the source position under different driving conditions, but we didn’t have them…

2. Anechoic recordings. Conversations among Italians, with two, three, and five or more speakers, were recorded in an anechoic chamber and could be placed in the VR scene as point sources.

3. Field recordings. We made recordings at Piazza Vittoria and in the surrounding area and added them to the VR scene as background sound.

4. Audio files from the internet or our own sound libraries, including birdsong, fountains and surf, added to the VR scene as point sources or background sound.

As for the sound rendering, because it had to run in real time as web-based VR, it was very basic. First, the whole VR scene was treated as a free field. All point sources were attenuated with a logarithmic volume–distance rolloff (equivalent to 1/r), and all background sounds with a linear volume–distance rolloff. See the video below for the result.

We simulated 2 street designs × 2 traffic control schemes = 4 scenarios (Figures 4 and 5). Through our web-based VR, the public could experience the landscape and soundscape of Piazza Vittoria under the different street designs and traffic control schemes. Of course, as I said earlier, our project was a demonstration and a proof of concept, and the quality of the VR, especially the auralization, still needed work. We had about 100 people complete an online questionnaire; their ratings of the VR quality are shown in Figure 6. Overall, the sound in our VR scenes was too thin and too monotonous: nothing like the hubbub of real Naples.

Figure 4. Two street designs: the existing street and a shared street

Figure 5. Two traffic control schemes: no restrictions and no motor vehicles

Figure 6. Ratings of VR quality

Unfortunately, I have not continued with this line of work since 2016. High-quality real-time auralization is still expensive, and it may not yet be mature enough for widespread use in urban design. But as software, hardware and auralization technology keep improving, and as planning and design pay more and more attention to the acoustic environment, I hope that in the not-too-distant future auralization will be as widely used as visualization, supporting better public participation and decision-making.

About the author: Like Jiang, University of Leeds, works mainly on urban transport and the environment, especially noise.
